Staged calibration of a patient‑specific Fontan model and an in‑silico test of biventricular conversion

What would it take for the left ventricle to carry the systemic circulation after the two ventricles are separated?

Jan Bureš
Radek Fučík·Sukran Erdem, MD·Nicholas Anderson, MD
Mohammad Tarique Hussain, MD·Radomír Chabiniok, MD
Department of Mathematics, FNSPE, Czech Technical University in Prague · UT Southwestern Medical Center and Children’s Health, Dallas

Fontan circulation

Its lumped-parameter model

Motivation

A healthy heart is two pumps in series. A Fontan circulation runs on one.

Healthy. One ventricle for the lungs, one for the body.

Fontan. The veins are connected straight to the lung arteries.

Why it matters

  • Built by surgery for children born with one usable pump.
  • The price: high venous pressure and little reserve to fill the ventricle.
  • Complications accumulate over the years.

The patient

Here the systemic veins bypass the heart, and two ventricles work as one pump.

This patient

  • Both veins feed the lung arteries, the lower one through a conduit without fenestration.
  • Native aortic atresia. A large septal defect links the ventricles (154 mL at end-diastole). They share a neo-aortic outlet.

Measured

Venous (Fontan) pressure, mean13 mmHg
Lung-artery pressure, right / left12 / 11 mmHg
Wedge pressure, used as atrial mean7 mmHg
Aortic pressure, mean63 mmHg
Net output at 89 beats per minute5.6 L/min
Left + right ventricle, end-diastole71 + 83 mL

The question

If surgeons separate the two ventricles, can the left one supply the body?

Today · Fontan

Proposed · two pumps again

  • Combined end-diastolic volume is 154 mL. Cardiac index (net output per body surface area) is 3.64 L/min/m².
  • After separation the left ventricle works alone. Today it holds 71 mL.
  • What it can then deliver cannot be measured before surgery.

Approach

Calibrate a model to today’s data. Then change the model and explore.

From anatomy to model

Each part of the circulation becomes a few lumped elements.

The atrial pressure is prescribed at both ends, so the loop stays open.

Time stepping

  • Implicit time stepping, 1 ms per step.
  • Each step is a nonlinear system for 17 unknowns, solved by Newton.
  • Beats are repeated until two agree: the periodic orbit.

The experiment

The conversion changes topology and geometry, not the tissue.

Kept without refitting: tissue parameters, outflow valve, arch and both body beds. Swept: filling pressure and heart rate. The earlier 22 % inlet leak is not carried over.

Result 1

With today’s vessels, mean aortic pressure falls from 64 to 43 mmHg.

Fontan model, shared ventricleleft ventricle alone, same vessels
Model outputFontanLeft ventricle alone
Mean aortic pressure, mmHg63.942.9
Cardiac index, L/min/m²3.692.68
End-diastolic volume, mL15470
Ejection fraction, %5467

Converted model: mean left-atrial pressure 7 mmHg, prescribed venous outlet 6 mmHg. All values are computed.

  • Ejection fraction rises: the ventricle ejects against a lower pressure.
  • With today’s vessels the model reaches only 43 mmHg. How much can the left ventricle pump at the measured 63 mmHg?

Result 2

Restoring today’s arterial pressure takes narrower vessels, and the modelled output falls to 2.45 L/min/m².

1Why

In a body, reflexes regulate arterial pressure: when it falls, the small arteries narrow. The model has no such reflex, so with today’s vessels it settles at 43 mmHg.

2What we do

We assume that today’s pressure is kept, and narrow both body beds by one factor k until the mean aortic pressure is back at 63 mmHg.

​Rj​→kRj​,Cj​→Cj​/kF(k)=PˉaAo​(k)−63 mmHg=0​

3What it costs

Narrower vessels are a heavier load. With heart rate and filling fixed, the output falls from 2.68 to 2.45 L/min/m².

An imposed constraint, not a model of the reflex.

Result 3

The output depends on filling pressure, heart rate and assumed reserve.

Heart rate per minute, labelled at the curves
100 / minnominalcontractility +25 %smaller, stiffer wall

How it was used

An operating map for the clinical discussion: each output level has a filling and heart-rate cost.

preferredintermediateconcern

Zones: the clinicians’ discussion categories, not validated thresholds.

  • What it is for. After surgery, clinicians can influence both axes. Heart ratepacing or drugs can adjust it. Filling pressurean infusion into a vein can raise it. Drugs that increase urine output can lower it.
  • How to read it. A target output is a line. 3.0 is reached in the preferred zone; 3.5 needs about 11 mmHg at 110 per minute.

Message for the clinical team: continue the assessment. The model alone does not justify a go-ahead.

Summary

At rest, the modelled left ventricle pumps about two-thirds of today’s output.

We fitted a lumped-parameter Fontan model to one patient’s MRI and catheter data.

The model prescribes filling pressure. Can the right ventricle and lungs sustain it?

Backup · calibration details

What each calibration stage assumes and fits.

Stage 1 · resistances

  • Mean flows are made mass-consistent first.
  • Mean pressures at four sites: 63, 61, 13 and 7 mmHg.
  • Four totals follow: arch, upper body, lower body, lungs.
  • The split 1 : 10 : 1 inside a body bed is assumed.

Stage 2 · compliances

  • Solved per harmonic, for the measured aortic inflow.
  • Four log-scales s of grouped compliances and six bounded phase shifts are fitted to six waveforms.
  • A quadratic penalty on the log-scales favours the reference compliances from the earlier fit.
  • Two capacitors on the aortic node enter only as their sum.

Stage 3 · heart

  • Sphere from measured volumes, one passive scale from the end-diastolic point.
  • Then contractility, activation and valve parameters: ten in all.
  • Outflow inertance ends within 0.03 % of its upper bound.
  • The selected set passes all declared adequacy tests. It is not claimed to be a global minimum.

Backup · discretisation

Selected time-discrete residuals, as implemented in PhysioBlocks.

Notation: Δz=zn+1−zn, Dh​z=Δz/Δt, zˉ=21​(zn+1+zn), zγ​=zˉ+γΔz.

Velocity law
Dh​y˙​=y¨​0.4​,Dh​y=y˙​ˉ​+40.42​ΔtΔy¨​
Wall
ρ0​Dh​y˙​+ΔyΔWe​​+R0​Σv​(yˉ​,Dh​y)​+R0​ks​​(R0​yˉ​​−eˉc​)=∣Ω0​∣Pˉ−Pˉext​​ΔyΔV​
Valve
LDh​Q+G(Q0.25​)Q0.25​​=Pˉup​−Pˉdown​
Active law
Dh​Kc​=−(∣un+1∣+α∣Dh​ec​∣)Kcn+1​+n0​(ecn​)K0​u+n+1​,Tc♯​=Kcn+1​​λˉc​

For ∣Δy/yn∣≤10−6 the two quotients are replaced by analytic derivatives at the midpoint.

Solver

  • Midpoint pressures, weighted velocity and valve updates, secant quotients ΔWe​/Δy and ΔV/Δy.
  • Newton on scaled residuals, tolerance 10−8. A failed step is subdivided, down to Δt/16.

Acceptance of a periodic solution, Fontan model

  • The last two beats differ by at most 0.02 mmHg, 0.02 mL and 0.2 mL/s.
  • Volume balance per beat below 0.1 mL.
  • Cavity volume and radii stay positive along the whole transient.
  • Paired run at Δt/2, seven traces at three heart rates: largest RMS difference 0.31 % of the waveform range, largest pointwise difference 1.3 %.

Backup · Stage 3 objective

The heart-stage residual and how the parameter set was selected.

J3​(θ)=240 waveform residualsj=1∑3​801​i=0∑79​[0.1range(yj​)eji∘​(θ)​]2​​+10 scalarsℓ=1∑10​(sℓ​bℓ​(θ)−bℓ⋆​​)2​​+4 one-sided penaltiesm=1∑4​πm​(θ)2​​

eji​=y^​j​(ti​+δj​;θ)−yj​(ti​). For the aortic flow the cycle mean of e is removed, e∘=e−⟨e⟩. For the two pressures e∘=e.

  • Three waveforms at their own periods. Each delay δj​ is found by a bounded search, ∣δj​∣≤0.1Tj​, at every evaluation.
  • Ten scalars: mean and peak flow, end-diastolic volume, two leak fractions, five pressure values.
  • Bounded trust-region least squares, forward-difference Jacobian with 1 % steps, warm-started orbits.
  • Selected set, checked from a cold start: J3​=5.86 at 1 ms and 5.88 at 0.5 ms.
  • It passes all declared adequacy tests on both grids, with every delay strictly inside its bound.
  • It is a feasible point chosen after the bounded search. It does not improve every waveform of the earlier fit.

Backup · pressure restoration

The load factor is found by a safeguarded scalar root search.

F(k)=T1​∫0T​PaAo​(t;k)dt−63 mmHg=0
  • Each evaluation of F is a full periodic orbit of the coupled model. The output is free to change.
  • Start at k=1, then 3 or 0.5 to bracket the root. Then secant steps, safeguarded inside the bracket.
  • Tolerance ±0.25 mmHg, at most eight evaluations. Here six: k=1, 3, 1.939, 1.746, 1.686, 1.711.
  • Only the mean is prescribed. The pressure waveform and the output are computed.
  • Six bed resistances are multiplied and their six compliances divided by k, so every Rj​Cj​ is kept. The arch is fixed.

Backup · pressure and flow

The operating point is where the ventricle meets the vascular load.

  • Straight lines: mean aortic pressure = outlet pressure + vascular resistance × mean flow.
  • Teal: periodic orbits of the converted model as k grows from 1 to 3, at 89 per minute and 7 mmHg filling.
  • The factor k turns the load line. The root is the k whose line meets the ventricle at 63 mmHg.
  • The Fontan beds drain at 13 mmHg, not 6, so that point lies above the line for k=1.

Backup · why the model was refitted

An earlier fit matched the data and still produced an artefact after conversion.

earlier fitrefitted model
  • Earlier fit: a late pressure rebound of 7.7 mmHg at the end of ejection. Nothing in the Fontan fit showed it.
  • Mechanism in the model: outflow inertance keeps blood moving against an adverse pressure gradient while activation outlasts ejection.
  • Refitting inertance and activation shape together removes it: below 0.2 mmHg. The mean of the three squared waveform NRMSEs rises by 1.6 %.
  • Resting cardiac index changes from 2.39 to 2.45. Over 30 matched points of the map the change is between −7.3 % and +2.6 %.
  • No measured loop exists after conversion. The feature is model-dependent, and the fit alone could not reveal it.
